newsitem.title: UK: Boeing head says defense spending behind bid.
newsitem.headline: Boeing head says defense spending behind bid.

text.p: Boeing Co. bid for McDonnell Douglas Corp. because it believes defence spending could start to grow again and it wants to benefit from a larger military business, its chief executive was quoted as saying Thursday.

Philip Condit, who became Boeing's chief executive in April and takes over as chairman next month, told the Financial Times he did not believe it was a mistake to undertake a major expansion when defence spending was falling.
"If I was making a five-year decision, I would say there would be real questions. But I'm looking 20 to 30 years ahead," Condit was quoted as saying.
"Much as I would like to say that we will never see defence spending rise again, history tells us that's not true," he said in an interview.

Condit told the newspaper that he had not received any guarantees from Washington that the takeover, which would turn the new company into the world's largest defence and aerospace group in terms of sales, would be approved.
But it quoted him as saying there was little overlap between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, which would make it easier for regulators to approve the deal.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has said the European Commission would have to assess whether the deal would strengthen Boeing's dominant position in Europe.

A report last month in the Financial Times said Boeing moved swiftly on the bid because it feared McDonnell Douglas was about to bid for the defence operations of General Motors Corp.'s Hughes Electronics.
The newspaper said Condit did not deny this, but explained that his concern had been broader.

"I looked at things that were starting to move, and maybe move rapidly, in the next phase of defence industry consolidation," he said. "If we waited to see where it went, we might have been in a position where the cards had all been played."
